blocks.md: The coefficient of variation measures spread relative to the average. The standard deviation alone depends on units — if every income doubled, it would double too, even though nobody would say inequality had doubled. Dividing by the mean fixes that: a coefficient of 0.3 means incomes typically differ from the average by about thirty percent, whatever the currency or price level.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It lets you compare dispersion across groups, countries or years with different average incomes.
The standard deviation divided by the mean.

sections.heading: Why not just the standard deviation?

blocks.md: The SD depends on the units. If every income doubles, the SD doubles, but nobody would say inequality doubled. Dividing by the mean makes the measure **scale invariant**.
**Worked example**: for the nine wages in [Defining Inequality](note:defining-inequality), population SD = 4.36 and mean = 13.89, so $CV = 0.31$.

| Property | CV |
| --- | --- |
| Scale invariant | Yes |
| Transfer principle | Yes |
| Sensitivity | Equal weight everywhere — so in practice dominated by the **top**, where deviations are large |
| Decomposable | Its square, $\tfrac12 CV^2$, is a member of the decomposable generalized-entropy family |
